title: Comparing and ordering measurements
keyIdea: Measure first, then compare the numbers with their units. Start a ruler at 0, read scales carefully, and use the same unit for both things. Record the result with > (greater than), < (less than) or = (the same), and order several measurements from smallest to greatest.
familyTip: Measure three things at home, such as a spoon, a sock and a book, in centimetres. Write the results with < or >, then put them in order. Weigh a big light thing and a small heavy thing on kitchen scales and ask which is heavier before you look.

visual.caption: Which symbol fits each pair of measurements? Drag each card into >, = or <, or tap the card then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide a ribbon to 0 on a ruler, weigh a box and a tin, pour two jugs, order three strings and compare 1 m with 90 cm.

kid: To compare two things, measure them both. Then look at the numbers and the units. Put the start of the thing at 0 on the ruler. Then read the number at the end. If it starts at 4 and ends at 16, it is 12 cm, not 16 cm.
Write what you find with a sign. 45 cm > 32 cm means 45 cm is more. 150 g < 400 g means 150 g is less. 500 ml = 500 ml means they are the same.
Big does not always mean heavy. A big box of popcorn can be lighter than a small tin. A tall jug can hold the same as a wide jug. Measure to find out.
Use the same unit for both. 1 m is 100 cm, so 1 m is more than 90 cm. To put three in order, start with the smallest number.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. National Curriculum in England, Year 2 measurement: compare and order lengths, mass, volume and capacity, and record the results using >, < and =. Children measure in standard units (cm and m, g and kg, ml and litres) first.

A comparison is only fair when both measurements are taken correctly and are in the same unit. Length is read from a 0 start, or found as the difference between start and end. Mass and capacity are read from scales. The symbols then record the comparison of the two measurements.

Common mistakes: reading only the end mark when the object does not start at 0; judging mass by size (bigger means heavier) or capacity by height (taller means holds more) instead of measuring; comparing numbers in different units (thinking 90 cm is longer than 1 m because 90 > 1); and turning the < or > sign the wrong way.

In the lab your child slides a ribbon to the 0 mark, records 45 cm > 32 cm, weighs a big box and a small tin, pours a tall jug and a wide jug into a measuring jug, orders three strings that do not start in line, and changes 1 m into 100 cm before comparing it with 90 cm.

practice.hint: Which length is more? The open side of the sign faces the bigger one.
practice.explain: 45 is more than 32, so 45 cm > 32 cm.

practice.prompt: A crayon starts at {s} cm and ends at {e} cm on a ruler. How long is the crayon in cm?
practice.hint: It does not start at 0. Find the gap from the start to the end.
practice.explain: From {s} to {e} is {=e-s}, so the crayon is {=e-s} cm long.

practice.prompt: A big box weighs 150 g. A small tin weighs 400 g. Which is heavier?
practice.hint: Compare the grams, not the sizes.
practice.explain: 400 g is more than 150 g, so the small tin is heavier: 150 g < 400 g.

practice.prompt: Jug A holds {a} ml. Jug B holds {b} ml. How many more ml does jug A hold?
practice.hint: Find the difference: take the smaller amount from the bigger one.
practice.explain: {a} ml take away {b} ml is {=a-b} ml, so jug A holds {=a-b} ml more.

practice.prompt: Which is longer: 1 m or 90 cm?
practice.explain: 1 m is 100 cm, and 100 cm is more than 90 cm, so 1 m > 90 cm.

pool.prompt: Put in order, shortest first: 15 cm, 9 cm, 22 cm
pool.explain: 9 is the smallest and 22 is the biggest: 9 cm < 15 cm < 22 cm.

pool.prompt: A tall jug and a wide jug both fill a measuring jug to 500 ml. Which symbol fits: tall ? wide
pool.hint: Look at the measurements, not the shapes.
pool.explain: Both hold 500 ml, so they hold the same: 500 ml = 500 ml.

pool.hint: Which mass is less? The sign points to the smaller one.
pool.explain: 3 is less than 5, so 3 kg < 5 kg.

pool.prompt: Sam says 90 cm is longer than 1 m because 90 is more than 1. What went wrong?
choices: He used the wrong sign only
pool.explain: 1 m is 100 cm. Compare 100 cm with 90 cm: 1 m is longer.

pool.prompt: A ribbon is {a} cm long. A string is {b} cm long. How much longer is the ribbon in cm?
pool.hint: Take the shorter length from the longer one.
pool.explain: {a} cm take away {b} cm is {=a-b} cm.

pool.prompt: A pencil starts at 2 and ends at 10 on a ruler. Which is true?
pool.hint: It did not start at 0. Count the gap from 2 to 10.
pool.explain: From 2 to 10 is 8 cm, and 8 cm < 10 cm.

pool.prompt: Parcel A weighs {a} g. Parcel B weighs {b} g. How many grams heavier is parcel B?
pool.hint: Parcel B has more grams. Take A's grams from B's grams.
pool.explain: {b} g take away {a} g is {=b-a} g, so {a} g < {b} g and B is {=b-a} g heavier.

pool.hint: 60 and 6 share a digit, but which is more?
pool.explain: 60 is ten times 6, so 60 cm > 6 cm.
